title: Alternative Protein Food Products
desc: Plan a small food product built on plant, fungal or insect protein: recipe, safety, labelling, costing and honest claims.
outcomes: Explain protein sources and the nutrition and allergy basics.
Scale a recipe and plan a safe process.
Compare taste, cost and nutrition against a normal product.
Run a tasting test and write a launch plan.
task: Develop one alternative-protein product to a tested recipe with hygiene plan, label draft, cost sheet and tasting results.
condition: A clean kitchen or partner food unit, scales, a spreadsheet, 10 tasters, two peers and a food-trade mentor. Local food rules are checked.
standard: Recipe is repeatable within 5% weight; allergen list is complete; hygiene plan passes; label meets local rules; cost per pack is shown; 10 tasters' scores recorded; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Food entrepreneurs, cooks, product developers, hospitality staff.
evidence: recipe card, hygiene plan, label draft, cost sheet, tasting record
modules: Protein sources
Understand
Many foods can provide protein. A good alternative-protein product uses sources well.
Pulses, grains, soy, nuts and seeds, mushroom-based protein, algae and insects are all used.
Combining sources, such as rice with lentils, supplies a more complete amino acid profile.
Protein per 100 g varies widely; read labels and use recognised data.
Some sources need special processing to remove bitter or harmful compounds.
Rice and lentils together give a more complete protein than either alone. A batch of lentil patties provides about 9 g protein per 100 g.
Make a table of six sources with protein per 100 g from labels, with the date.
Values come from labels or recognised tables.
Nutrition and allergy
Analyse
A product must be nutritious and safe for people with allergies.
Check iron, B12, calcium, fibre, salt and fat balance.
Major allergens: soy, nuts, gluten, milk, eggs, fish and shellfish; insect protein can cross-react with shellfish allergy.
Declare allergens in bold on the label.
Prevent cross-contact in the kitchen.
An insect-flour product warns on the label that people with shellfish allergy should avoid it and that it is made in a unit that also handles nuts.
Check your recipe against an allergen list and write the allergen statement.
All allergens named and cross-contact controls listed.
Recipe development
Create
Test small, change one thing at a time and record everything.
Weigh all ingredients and record steps with time and temperature.
Make three batches and compare.
Adjust salt, texture and moisture gradually.
Record batch numbers and dates.
Version 3 uses 18% less salt and holds shape better after a 2-minute longer rest. The three batches vary by 3% in weight.
Write a recipe card and make three batches.
Batches within 5% weight and tasting notes recorded.
Hygiene and food safety
Apply
Prevent harm with controls at the right steps.
Identify hazards and control points such as cooking temperature and cooling time.
Keep raw and cooked separate; clean tools and surfaces.
Use thermometers and record temperatures.
Train all staff and keep logs.
Cooked patties are cooled from 60 to 21 degrees within 2 hours and then to 5 degrees within a further 4 hours, with times logged.
Write a hygiene and control plan with measurable limits.
Each control point has a limit and a record.
Labels and claims
Evaluate
The label must tell the truth.
Name, ingredients by weight, allergens, net weight, date, storage, maker details.
Claims such as "high protein" must meet rules for the amount.
Use "meat-free" or "vegan" only if true.
Check local rules with an adviser.
A label lists "Contains soy" in bold, net weight 250 g, best-before date and storage "keep refrigerated, use within 3 days of opening".
Draft a label for your product and get adviser comments.
Label meets local rules per adviser check.
Costing and price
Analyse
Know your cost per pack and your margin.
Ingredients, packing, fuel, labour, loss and overhead.
Price above cost with a margin; compare with normal products.
Account for waste and test batches.
Review costs when prices change.
A 250 g pack costs 42 INR to make. Sold at 70 INR, margin is 28 INR. A 10% price rise in lentils changes cost to 44 INR.
Build a cost sheet.
Totals are correct and currency is shown.
Taste test and feedback
Evaluate
Use real tasters and real scores.
Ask 10 tasters to score taste, texture, appearance and value from 1 to 5.
Ask about allergies and get consent.
Record comments without defending.
Change one thing and test again.
Texture scores 3.2. Mixing time is reduced by one minute and the next test scores 4.1.
Run a tasting test and record scores.
Scores and changes logged.
Launch plan
Create
Start small and learn.
Choose a channel: market, cafe, online.
Plan cold storage and delivery.
Plan packaging that can be reused or recycled.
Set targets for sales and complaints.
A weekend market stall with samples sells 60 packs and collects 25 email sign-ups.
Write the launch plan.
Plan includes costs, channels and a review date.
quiz: Why combine protein sources?
To get all amino acids. (Covered in module 1: Protein sources. To pass that module: Values from labels with the date.)
Name two allergens.
Soy and nuts (also gluten, shellfish cross-reaction). (Covered in module 2: Nutrition and allergy. To pass that module: All allergens named.)
What goes on a label?
Name, ingredients, allergens, weight, date, storage, maker. (Covered in module 3: Recipe development. To pass that module: Batches within 5% weight.)
Why weigh ingredients?
For repeatable batches. (Covered in module 4: Hygiene and food safety. To pass that module: Controls measurable.)
What is a control point?
A step like cooking temperature that prevents harm. (Covered in module 5: Labels and claims. To pass that module: Meets local rules per adviser check.)
How cool cooked food?
Quickly, within the rule. (Covered in module 6: Costing and price. To pass that module: Totals correct; currency shown.)
How many tasters here?
At least 10. (Covered in module 7: Taste test and feedback. To pass that module: Scores and changes logged.)
Name a cost item.
Ingredients, packing, fuel, labour, loss, overhead. (Covered in module 8: Launch plan. To pass that module: Plan includes cost, channels and a review date.)
When say meat-free?
Only when true. (Covered in module 8: Launch plan. To pass that module: Plan includes cost, channels and a review date.)
What do you log?
Batches, temperatures, cleaning. (Covered in module 8: Launch plan. To pass that module: Plan includes cost, channels and a review date.)

ladder: Protein sources

L1: learner can name protein sources. Focus module: Protein sources (Understand, 4 h). Many sources can make a balanced protein. Key points: Pulses, grains, soy, mushrooms-based protein, algae and insects. Combine sources to give all amino acids. Know the typical protein per 100 g.

Teach: open with the worked example. Rice with lentils gives a more complete protein than either alone. Then set the activity: Make a table of 6 sources with protein per 100 g. Mark against the standard: Values from labels with the date. Check at this level: Why combine protein sources? Model answer: To get all amino acids. Show samples.
Nutrition and allergy

L2: learner knows allergens and hygiene. Focus module: Nutrition and allergy (Analyse, 5 h). Healthy and safe for everyone. Key points: Check iron, B12, calcium, salt and fat balance. Allergens: soy, nuts, gluten, shellfish cross-reaction with insects. Show allergens in bold on the label.

Teach: open with the worked example. An insect-flour product warns people with shellfish allergy. Then set the activity: Check your recipe against an allergen list. Mark against the standard: All allergens named. Check at this level: Name two allergens. Model answer: Soy and nuts (also gluten, shellfish cross-reaction). Allergen list.
Recipe development

L3: learner can follow a recipe card. Focus module: Recipe development (Create, 6 h). Test small, repeat exactly. Key points: Weigh everything; write steps with time and temperature. Change one thing at a time. Record batch numbers.

Teach: open with the worked example. Version 3 uses 18% less salt and tastes the same. Then set the activity: Write a recipe card and make 3 batches. Mark against the standard: Batches within 5% weight. Check at this level: What goes on a label? Model answer: Name, ingredients, allergens, weight, date, storage, maker. Weigh together.
Hygiene and food safety

L4: learner can run a batch with logs. Focus module: Hygiene and food safety (Apply, 5 h). Prevent harm before it happens. Key points: Identify hazards and control points such as cooking temperature and cooling time. Clean surfaces, tools and hands; separate raw and cooked. Keep temperature and cleaning logs.

Teach: open with the worked example. Cooked patties are cooled from 60 to 21 degrees within two hours. Then set the activity: Write a hygiene and control plan. Mark against the standard: Controls measurable. Check at this level: Why weigh ingredients? Model answer: For repeatable batches. Run a batch.
Labels and claims

L5: learner can cost, label and test. Focus module: Labels and claims (Evaluate, 5 h). Say what is true. Key points: Name, ingredients by weight, allergens, net weight, date, storage, maker. Claims such as "high protein" need the numbers to match rules. Use "meat-free" only when true.

Teach: open with the worked example. A label says "contains soy" in bold and gives best-before date. Then set the activity: Draft a label. Mark against the standard: Meets local rules per adviser check. Check at this level: What is a control point? Model answer: A step like cooking temperature that prevents harm. Cost sheet.
Taste test and feedback

L6: learner can lead a kitchen shift. Focus module: Taste test and feedback (Evaluate, 4 h). Real tasters, real scores. Key points: 10 tasters score taste, texture, look, fairness of price from 1 to 5. Record comments; do not defend. Tasters give consent and are asked about allergies.

Teach: open with the worked example. Texture is scored 3.2; mixing time is adjusted. Then set the activity: Run a tasting test. Mark against the standard: Scores and changes logged. Check at this level: How cool cooked food? Model answer: Quickly, within the rule. Cover rota.
Launch plan

L7: learner can audit a food plan. Focus module: Launch plan (Create, 5 h). Small first sales. Key points: Choose a channel: market, cafe, online. Plan cold storage and delivery. Plan packaging that can be reused or recycled.

Teach: open with the worked example. Weekend market stall with samples sells 60 packs. Then set the activity: Write the launch plan. Mark against the standard: Plan includes cost, channels and a review date. Check at this level: How many tasters here? Model answer: At least 10. Peer audit.
